target.title: Auto-AVSR: Audio-Visual Speech Recognition with Automatic Labels

read.pdf: Fig. 1 and Tables 1–5 read in the supplied full-text extraction; separate PDF not supplied

entries.text: The authors say their public pretrained ASR models generated automatic labels for more than 2,000 hours of unlabelled video.
entries.condition: Automatically transcribed unlabelled AVSpeech and VoxCeleb2 English subsets; pseudo-transcripts are used as training labels.

entries.text: The English-filtered AVSpeech subset contains 1,323 hours.
entries.condition: AVSpeech; English subset selected using VoxLingua107 language classification; training data with automatic transcripts.
entries.quote: resulting in a total of 1 323 hours

entries.quote: comprises 1 307 data hours

entries.text: The abstract claims a 30% relative improvement over the current state-of-the-art approach, without naming the denominator in that sentence.

entries.text: The abstract claims performance above methods trained on non-public data with 26 times more training data.

entries.quote: trained on non-publicly available datasets with 26 times more

entries.text: The proposed approach uses a pretrained ASR system to create pseudo-labels and incorporates them directly into training, rather than requiring the two-stage SSL route or teacher distillation.
entries.condition: Self-training-style label generation using publicly available pretrained ASR; the authors say the process avoids costly iterative self-training and can be combined with SSL.

entries.text: The authors claim direct pseudo-label training simplifies implementation and reduces the computational and memory costs of using a teacher during training.
entries.condition: Comparison is with teacher-based distillation during target-model training; no measured compute or memory values are reported.

entries.text: The authors present public datasets and models as facilitating reproducibility and comparison.
entries.condition: The paper links its code and trained models at the GitHub repository recorded in target.read.code.

entries.text: The authors report that pretrained-ASR WER on LibriSpeech is not highly correlated with downstream ASR/VSR performance from its transcripts.
entries.condition: Comparison uses four pretrained ASR systems; downstream models are trained on LRW, LRS2, LRS3, VoxCeleb2 and AVSpeech (3,448 h total) and evaluated on LRS3; teacher LibriSpeech metric is test-clean.

entries.text: Conformer-Transducer transcripts are used for the main experiments because they give the best average downstream ASR/VSR performance among the tested labelers.
entries.condition: Compared labelers: Conformer-Transducer, HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0 and Whisper; Table 1 downstream LRS3 experiments use 3,448 total training hours.
entries.quote:
we rely on the automatically-generated transcriptions from the
Conformer-Transducer [12] since on average it leads to the best per-
formance for both ASR and VSR models.

entries.text: HuBERT is the stated exception: its downstream models perform slightly worse despite HuBERT's strong LibriSpeech result.
entries.condition: HuBERT-generated labels; downstream audio-only and visual-only models evaluated on LRS3 after training on the 3,448 h corpus.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge that automatically generated transcripts inevitably contain noisy labels.
entries.condition: Unlabelled AVSpeech and VoxCeleb2 receive ASR-generated transcripts before supervised training.

entries.text: LRS2 has 144,482 clips and 225 total hours; its split counts and durations are reported below in pretraining, training, validation, test order.
entries.condition: LRS2, BBC-program footage; the test split is 1,243 clips and 0.5 h. The paper does not report test-speaker count or train/test speaker overlap.

entries.text: LRS3 has 151,819 TED clips and 439 total hours; split counts and durations are pretraining, training-validation, test order.
entries.value: 151,819 clips; 439 hours; splits 118,516/31,982/1,321 clips and 408/30/0.9 hours
entries.condition: LRS3 test split: 1,321 clips and 0.9 h; test-speaker count and speaker overlap with training datasets are not reported.

entries.text: AVSpeech has 4,700 total hours, of which 1,323 English hours are used; it contains YouTube segments in multiple languages.
entries.condition: AVSpeech [18]; English filtering by VoxLingua107 [19]; the English subset is used with automatically generated transcripts.

entries.text: VoxCeleb2 has 2,300 hours from more than 6,000 people; the English list used here contains 1,307 hours.
entries.condition: VoxCeleb2 [17]; English list from [7]; the English subset is used with automatically generated transcripts.

entries.text: Visual inputs are mouth-region crops; each frame is normalized with training-set mean and standard deviation, while audio is z-normalized per utterance.
entries.condition: Visual processing follows [22]; numeric training-set mean/std and the exact audio z-normalization formula are not specified in the paper.

entries.text: Training uses SentencePiece subwords, a 5,000-unit vocabulary, 75 epochs, AdamW, cosine learning-rate scheduling, 5 warm-up epochs, peak learning rate 1e-3, and a maximum 1,800 frames per batch.
entries.value: 5,000 units; 75 epochs; 5 warm-up epochs; peak lr 1e-3; 1,800 frames/batch
entries.unit: subword units; epochs; learning rate; frames
entries.condition: Implementation details for the models; the paper does not report random seeds or repeated runs.

entries.text: Visual augmentation uses horizontal flipping, random cropping and adaptive time masking; audio augmentation uses adaptive time masking; maximum mask length is 0.4 seconds.
entries.condition: Mask count is proportional to utterance length; modalities use the augmentation stated for their inputs.

entries.text: Visual-only models use a transformer language model trained on 166 million characters; ASR and AV-ASR omit language models because the authors observed no further improvement.
entries.condition: The corpus combines LibriSpeech train (960 h), LRS2/LRS3 pretraining and training sets, TED-LIUM 3, English Voxforge and English Common Voice; ASR and AV-ASR have no external LM according to the paper.
entries.quote:
language models are not included for ASR and A V-ASR
models since no further improvements are observed

entries.text: The visual front end is a modified ResNet-18 with a spatiotemporal first convolution; audio and visual encoders use Conformer back ends and are fused by an MLP before the CTC/attention decoder.
entries.value: 12 Conformer layers; 6 Transformer decoder layers; 2-layer fusion MLP; 243.1M ASR and 250.4M VSR parameters
entries.condition: VSR first convolution kernel 5×7×7 and stride 1×2×2; ASR front end is 1D ResNet-18; fusion MLP hidden/output sizes 8,192/768.

entries.text: Audio-only and visual-only front ends are pretrained on LRW before the reported downstream training.
entries.condition: Table 2 and Table 3/4 describe model initialization/data totals including LRW; final benchmark conditions vary by row.

entries.text: Conformer-Transducer teacher was trained with the 12,000-hour NeMo ASRSET; Whisper was trained on 680,000 hours of labelled audio.
entries.condition: Pretrained teacher model descriptions; these are source-model training amounts, not Auto-AVSR downstream training hours.

questions.q: What exactly is the headline 0.9% WER result, and what protocol details constrain interpretation?
questions.answer: It is the LRS3 test result for audio-visual Auto-AVSR trained with 3,448 total hours from LRW, LRS2, LRS3, VoxCeleb2 and AVSpeech; the paper says AV-ASR has no external LM. Speaker overlap, run seeds/repetitions and paper-run decoder settings are unstated. The public repository snapshot has later defaults and cannot establish that they produced this result.

questions.q: How do the reported WERs change as automatically transcribed data grows, and does every modality keep improving?
questions.answer: Table 2 shows visual-only WER falling from 33.0% to 19.1% over 0–2,630 additional hours, while audio-only WER falls from 1.5% to 1.0% and changes only marginally after 1,578 additional hours. The authors characterize ASR as approaching saturation.

questions.q: What baseline supports the abstract's 30% relative-improvement claim?
questions.answer: The abstract does not identify its denominator. Table 4 lists 1.4% for AV-HuBERT and 1.6% for ViT3D-CM on LRS3 audio-visual recognition, versus 0.9% for Auto-AVSR; the stated 30% cannot be tied unambiguously to either table entry from the paper text.

questions.q: How strong is the noise-robustness evidence, and what limitation do the authors flag?
questions.answer: Across the LRS3 noise table, audio-visual WER is lower than audio-only WER at each listed SNR for babble, pink and white noise. The authors caution that babble appears in both training and testing, which may explain the particularly low babble-noise error despite different SNR levels.
